reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Classic mechanisms are a dashboard injury (posteriorly directed force on a flexed knee) or a fall onto a flexed knee with a plantarflexed foot
The posterior drawer test is the most reliable examination sign, with a posterior sag observed in 90 degrees of flexion
Isolated PCL injuries are often treated non-operatively with quadriceps rehabilitation, unlike many ACL tears
High-grade or combined ligament injuries (especially with posterolateral corner injury) are more likely to require reconstruction
A PCL injury raises suspicion of a multiligament injury or a reduced knee dislocation with vascular risk
Quadriceps strengthening is central because the quadriceps dynamically substitutes for PCL function
Chronic deficiency can lead to patellofemoral and medial compartment osteoarthritis
reference.pathophysiology: The PCL is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation. A posteriorly directed force on the proximal tibia of a flexed knee, or hyperflexion, exceeds its tensile strength and tears it, usually in the mid-substance. Posterior tibial subluxation alters joint contact and, if combined with posterolateral corner injury, produces rotatory instability; long-standing deficiency increases patellofemoral and medial compartment loading.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior cruciate ligament injury (a false-positive anterior drawer from a posterior sag)
Multiligament knee injury or reduced dislocation
additionalInvestigations: Posterior drawer and posterior sag tests, with dial test for posterolateral corner
MRI of the knee to confirm and grade the tear
Stress radiographs to quantify posterior translation
Vascular assessment where a dislocation is suspected
Examination under anaesthesia for multiligament injuries
redFlags: Signs of knee dislocation with possible popliteal artery injury
Combined posterolateral corner injury producing gross rotatory instability
Common peroneal nerve palsy accompanying posterolateral injury
reference.prognosis: Isolated low-grade PCL injuries usually do well with rehabilitation; combined injuries have poorer outcomes and often need reconstruction, and chronic deficiency predisposes to osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Mistaking a posterior sag for a positive anterior drawer and diagnosing an ACL tear
Missing an associated posterolateral corner injury, which compromises PCL reconstruction
Overlooking a spontaneously reduced knee dislocation and its vascular risk
Neglecting quadriceps rehabilitation in non-operative management
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Manage isolated low-grade injuries non-operatively with a structured quadriceps-strengthening rehabilitation programme, as the quadriceps dynamically substitutes for posterior cruciate function
Use a dynamic posterior cruciate brace and protected weight-bearing in the early phase to limit posterior tibial sag during healing
Reserve surgical reconstruction for high-grade, symptomatic or combined ligament injuries, particularly with posterolateral corner involvement
Address associated posterolateral corner injury at the same operation to correct rotatory instability
Exclude and urgently manage an associated reduced knee dislocation, with vascular assessment for popliteal artery injury
Monitor for chronic instability and progressive patellofemoral and medial compartment osteoarthritis over time
Refer to orthopaedic or sports medicine services and physiotherapy for staged rehabilitation and return-to-sport criteria
